# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Blind, Mute, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [blue]
WIRES 1:[white] 2:[red] 3:[green] 4:[yellow] 5:[blue]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎 ☝]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👌 ✌]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝ 👌]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✌ 👎]

I need to think about this carefully. Mute has sent me gestures, likely encoding information from the manual - possibly mapping wire colors/numbers to actions, or asking me questions.

Since gestures came in pairs, this could be a code: first symbol = category, second = value. Let me consider they might be trying to establish a numbering system (👍=1, 👎=2, ☝=3, ✌=4, 👌=5, etc.) so they can reference wires by position.

Since I can't hear anything and this is turn 1, Mute doesn't know what I see yet. I should report the bomb's display first, since Mute can't see it and needs this info to consult the manual. I'll describe display, light color, and wire colors in order using speech (Blind and Mute can hear me).

```
speak(text="Display shows 0. Light is blue. Wires in order: 1 white, 2 red, 3 green, 4 yellow, 5 blue.")
```

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [blue]
WIRES 1:[white] 2:[red] 3:[green] 4:[yellow] 5:[blue]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 ☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ ☝]

Mute is gesturing to me again. This looks like it could be a coordinate/reference system: 👍 followed by five ☝ symbols. Since I described 5 wires in order (1 white, 2 red, 3 green, 4 yellow, 5 blue), this might be Mute confirming they received my wire info, or pointing to something specific.

Possibly 👍 means "acknowledged/yes" and the five ☝ could mean "wire 5" repeated for emphasis, or counting to wire position 5 (blue wire matches blue light - could be significant).

Since I can't hear Blind or Mute's speech, and Mute can't hear me confirm gestures don't carry words - I should just keep relaying visual info and wait to see if more context clarifies. Let me acknowledge receipt and continue giving useful visual details, but I have already given all info I can see. I'll wait for Blind's spoken info to arrive next round, since Blind may have data from touching the bomb.

I should not act rashly. Let me send a gesture back acknowledging receipt, since Mute can see gestures too... wait, Mute cannot see - Mute reads manual, cannot see gestures (only Deaf sees gestures, Mute receives them per the channel table: "When you gesture, Mute receives it"). So my gestures reach Mute.

I'll gesture back a simple acknowledgment.

```
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍"])
wait()
```

TURN 4
ACTION BOARD:

Since I don't have a shared code and Mute cannot hear my speech confirmations of gesture meaning (wait, Mute CAN hear my speech - Mute is not deaf to speech, only Deaf-monkey cannot hear). Let me recheck: "When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it." So my speech reaches Mute. Good - I can use speech to establish a code with Mute, while gestures are one-directional from Mute to me (Mute cannot see my gestures back... wait, can Mute see? Mute reads manual - Mute's restriction is "cannot speak or touch". Nothing says Mute can't see gestures. Let me check gesture rules: "Whoever can see receives it, whoever cannot receives blanks." Only Deaf can see. So Mute cannot see - my gestures back to Mute arrive as blanks only.

So I should respond via speech instead, since Mute can hear me. Let me propose using speech to communicate, since gestures from me are useless to Mute (blanks only, revealing only count/quantity).

```
speak(to="mute", text="I can hear nothing but I can speak, and you can hear me. My gestures back to you only show as blanks, so please continue gesturing to me, and I will answer in words. I see display 0, blue light, wires in order white red green yellow blue.")
```

TURN 5

Mute gestures to Deaf: [✊ ✊ ✊ ✊ ✊]

Mute keeps sending gesture pairs, seemingly independent of my speech (since gestures and speech are separate channels and Mute might be following a fixed script per turn, sending both before hearing my reply, given turn order Blind→Mute→Deaf, my speech this round would only be heard by Mute next round).

Wait - actually turn order is Blind, Mute, Deaf each round. My speech in turn 4 was sent as Deaf (last in the round), so it would reach Mute at the start of the next round (turn 5). But this turn 5 shows Mute's gestures - meaning Mute already acted this round before receiving my speech from turn 4? Let me reconsider: "Whatever you missed reaches you at the start of the next one." So Mute's turn 5 action happens using info from turn 4's Blind and... my speech from turn 4 (Deaf, last) would reach Mute at start of turn 5. So Mute's turn 5 gestures might already reflect having read my message.

The gestures ✊✊✊✊✊ (five of the same) could relate to the five wires - maybe Mute is asking me to confirm wire colors one more time, or indicating "cut wire" count needed, or matching each wire to a symbol category.

Since I can't decode without a key, let me try establishing an explicit protocol via speech, proposing a simple mapping (e.g., use gestures for numbers 1-5 corresponding to wire position, and I'll describe back).

```
speak(to="mute", text="I don't have a code to read your gestures yet. Please gesture one symbol per wire in the same order as your manual lists them, and I will match them to what I see: wire 1 white, wire 2 red, wire 3 green, wire 4 yellow, wire 5 blue, light blue, display 0.")
```

ACTION BOARD:

This is the exact same sequence of gestures as Turn 1! This strongly suggests Mute is repeating a fixed message, not responding to my speech in real-time — perhaps Mute's actions are scripted/predetermined per round based on the manual alone, not adapting to conversation. This could be a fixed encoding of manual instructions meant to always be sent this way, independent of dialogue.

Let me analyze the pattern:
- [👍 👍]
- [👎 ☝]
- [👌 ✌]
- [☝ 👌]
- [✌ 👎]

Five pairs — matching five wires! Each pair could encode (action, wire-reference) or (wire-color-code, instruction). Since I described wires as white, red, green, yellow, blue — maybe each pair corresponds to one wire in that order, encoding something like "cut/don't cut" plus a check value.

If first symbol of each pair encodes an action:
1. 👍 👍 - wire 1 (white)
2. 👎 ☝ - wire 2 (red)
3. 👌 ✌ - wire 3 (green)
4. ☝ 👌 - wire 4 (yellow)
5. ✌ 👎 - wire 5 (blue)

Notice symbols reused: 👍,👎,☝,✌,👌 — exactly 5 distinct symbols for 5 wires, appearing as first element in each pair in order: 👍,👎,👌,☝,✌ — that's a permutation of all 5. And second elements: 👍,☝,✌,👌,👎 — also a permutation.

This looks like Mute is encoding a mapping/permutation between wires - like "wire order to cut" or "wire color to actual identity" per the manual, using symbols to represent wire positions 1-5 without needing words. Since Mute cannot know my wire colors directly, but I already told Mute the colors via speech in turn 1 (before this exact gesture pattern repeated in turn 1 too — meaning this is likely Mute's very first scripted move, not responsive).

Given I can't be 100% sure of decode, best action: try to establish confirmed symbol-to-wire mapping by asking Mute (via speech) to confirm one pairing at a time, or just relay this pattern to Blind via speech since Blind might interpret it with the manual logic Mute is implying.

Actually — I should relay these gesture patterns to Blind as blanks won't help, but I can describe them in words to Blind since Blind can hear me!

```
speak(to="blind", text="Mute has repeatedly gestured me this exact five-pair sequence: thumbsup-thumbsup, thumbsdown-index, ok-peace, index-ok, peace-thumbsdown. I think each pair corresponds to one wire in my listed order: white, red, green, yellow, blue. I don't know what the symbols mean numerically yet.")
speak(to="mute", text="I see the same five pairs again: thumbsup thumbsup, thumbsdown index, ok peace, index ok, peace thumbsdown. Are these one pair per wire, in the order white red green yellow blue? If so what do the symbols mean - please assign each symbol a number 1 to 5 by repeating that symbol that many times so I can learn the code.")
```
